nt: Meddah from Dishna, Qena, nicknamed Rayhanat al-Maddahin; the first Arab munshid to play the Châtelet in Paris after Umm Kulthum. Sources describe his mawlid and hadra performances but do not state the instrumentation, so it is left unresolved rather than guessed.

w: Ya Hamam Bitnuh Leh; Farsh wa Ghata; Madad ya Madad
nt: Blind meddah of Isna, Luxor, who sang the qisas — religious story-epics mixed with madih — over duff and tabl in the dhikr-circle manner; teacher of Mohamed Al-Ajuz.

w: Ashkuruka wa Arfuduk; Mawwal Yalli Han Dam'i
nt: Born Mohamed Ali Ahmed Adam in Naj' Hilal, Adfu, Aswan; trained by his uncle Ahmed Breen and sang madih over a mawlid percussion ensemble before moving toward sentimental sha'bi song.
Meddah of al-Dayr Sharq, Isna, who toured London and Paris; seven of his sons continue the family ensemble. The sources give no instrument list, so instrumentation is unresolved.
Asyut meddah styled Maddah al-Rasul, who formed his own inshad firqa and has played the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris. Documented by one source only.

w: Sira of al-Badawi; Sira of al-Disuqi; Death of the Prophet
nt: Qena meddah, born around 1935 and retired by 2018, described as a throat that chants without music: the clearest a cappella case in the Upper Egyptian tradition. His hour-long Death of the Prophet is the centrepiece of his repertoire.
Remembered master of the Qena hadra and the Laythi repertoire, held up in Upper Egyptian writing as the a cappella ideal — the more he used the voice unaided, the greater the mastery.
Named among the great Qena meddahs alongside Ahmed Al-Touni, with no further biography or repertoire documented; instrumentation unresolved.
Dishna meddah remembered as the teacher of Amin Al-Dishnawi; nothing further is documented and his instrumentation is unresolved.
The best-known munshid of the Nile Delta, outside the Sa'id tradition, singing mawwal and sharh over the public-hadra takht. Documented in the standard survey of Egyptian inshad.
Cairo munshid who has held a weekly Saturday session at the shrine of Sidi Ali Zayn al-Abidin; documented in the academic survey of Egyptian inshad, with instrumentation unspecified.

Cassette-era munshid who recorded the whole of al-Burdah as vocal solo with choral refrains; his home town is unverified, so the Sa'id attribution rests on the repertoire rather than a documented birthplace.

Upper Egyptian epic singer of the Sirat Bani Hilal over rabab and arghul — a neighbouring tradition rather than inshad, included because the meddah repertoire and the epic share performers and patrons. Locality unverified.
